- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecast is flat or rising slowly, adjust upward by 1–2% to account for sentiment-driven momentum.  
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) and forecast is rising, reduce forecast by 1–3% to avoid overcorrection.  
- After a sharp spike in price (true outcome > 85), model often overestimates continuation; cap forecast at +10% above peak for next 3–5 periods.  
- If official event net supply is negative and sentiment is bullish, model tends to overestimate; apply downward bias of 2–5% to offset bullish sentiment.  
- If sentiment is mixed (0.33–0.67) and forecast is trending, apply mean reversion: if forecast > 1.5σ above recent mean, reduce by 0.5–1.0σ.  
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if true outcome shows volatility > 5% from 10d mean, reduce forecast slope by 0.1–0.3 to avoid overfitting to recent spikes.  
- When supply net is negative and bullish sentiment is high, forecast should not exceed 1.2x recent 10d high unless confirmed by policy or auction data.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated negative spikes (e.g., -0.33 or lower) followed by recovery, model often underestimates rebound; add 0.5–1.0% buffer to forecast for next 3 periods.
